newsitem.title: USA: Moody's sets Ecuador on par with Argentina, Brazil.
newsitem.headline: Moody's sets Ecuador on par with Argentina, Brazil.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service stirred financial markets on Thursday when it rated Ecuador's long-term foreign currency debt at B1, the same level as Argentina and Brazil.
Wall Street revelled in the news, sending Ecuador's bond prices soaring and sparking forecasts that Moody's may soon upgrade Brazil and Argentina's credit standings.
"It's excellent news for Ecuador, and excellent news for people holding its assets," said Marco Santamaria, vice president at ING Barings.

Santamaria said Ecuador's rating was justified by the stability of fiscal policy, the record of steady economic growth and the fact it has never undergone the hyperinflation that has plagued other economies in the region.
"The defining feature of the economy is that it has been fairly stable over the time," Santamaria said.

The rating action sparked an immediate surge in Ecuador's Brady bonds, as Ecuador's discount bonds ECDISC=RR stormed close to three points higher to 77-3/8, while the country's par bonds ECPARS=RR gained 1-3/4 points to 53-1/4.
"I think there is still some more upside," said Gary Evans, global emerging market stretegist at UBS Securities. "Ecuador being rated brings in a lot more new money"
Evans linked the first time rating to Ecuador's record levels of reserves and a current account surplus.
But Jose Barrionuevo, head of emerging market research at Lehman Brothers, said he was surprised that Moody's would put Ecuador on a par with Argentina and Brazil.

Deteriorating monetary conditions, a debt/gross domestic product ratio near 80 percent and an elevated rate of debt service as a share of current account receivables should have set Ecuador apart from Argentina and Brazil, Barrionuevo said.
"This is an unfavorable surprise," Barrionuevo said. "This is a clear departure from Moody's previous practices of focusing heavily on debt indicators."

In its statement on Ecuador, Moody's said the rating reflected the "still-heavy burden of external debt on the economy and its concerns over the willingness to meet foreign currency obligations in a timely manner."
Wall Street analysts concurred that upgrades for the largest South American economies would not be long in coming.
"Investors should focus on Argentina and Brazil in terms of a near-term credit upgrade by Moody's," Barrionuevo said.
"There is going to be upward pressure on Argentina and Brazil to be upgraded," Evans said.
While Moody's maintains a B1 standing for the two largest South American economies, Standard and Poor's maintains a BB long-term sovereign rating for Argentina and a BB-minus rating for Brazil.
